results.title: Fracture Toughness Testing - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Fracture toughness testing refers to methods used to determine the fracture toughness of materials, often by introducing a controlled defect, such as a notch or indentation, before subjecting the specimen to bending tests. These methods evaluate the material's resistance to crack propagation under specific loading conditions. Fracture toughness tests provide quantification of a material's resistance to crack extension using the principles of fracture mechanics in both linear-elastic and elastic–plastic forms. Linear elastic fracture toughness tests are used to measure resistance to crack extension for metals which are relatively strong and have relatively low toughness. For this case, the region of plastic deformation associated with the crack is small relative to the dimensions of the crack and the test specimen, and linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) principles may be applied. In LEFM, the local stress field ahead of the tip of a sharp crack is characterised by the stress intensity parameter, K, which is dependent on the crack length, geometry, and applied load.

results.title: On the fracture toughness testing for single-edge notched bend specimen of orthotropic materials - ScienceDirect
results.content: # On the fracture toughness testing for single-edge notched bend specimen of orthotropic materials. Evaluate the SIF and CMOD for SENB specimens of orthotropic materials using 2D FEA. Majority of the fracture toughness tests on orthotropic materials reported in the literature are based on the testing methods developed for isotropic materials since there is no available testing standards specifically dealing with orthotropic materials. In this study, a systematic two-dimensional finite element analyses (2D FEA) of orthotropic single-edge notched bend (SENB) specimens are performed to evaluate the stress intensity factor (SIF) and crack mouth opening displacement (CMOD), which are two key parameters used in the fracture toughness tests. The research outcome is expected beneficial to the standardization of the fracture toughness testing on orthotropic composite materials such as wood, bone and unidirectional fiber-reinforced polymer composites. Fracture toughness tests are commonly conducted on small-scale specimens such as the single-edge notched bend (SENB or SE(B)) and compact tension (C(T)) specimens, which are specified in testing standards such as ASTM E399 [1] and E1820 [2].

Title: Fracture toughness determination for epoxy-based polymer concrete mixtures: Applicability of different rectangular beam and circular disc specimens - ScienceDirect
## Composites Part C: Open Access. Volume 14, July 2024, 100446. # Fracture toughness determination for epoxy-based polymer concrete mixtures: Applicability of different rectangular beam and circular disc specimens. Author links open overlay panel, , , , , , , ,. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcomc.2024.100446Get rights and content. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Abstract. The purpose of this study was to examine the potential impact of the testing procedure, the shape of the test sample, loading method and sample size on the *K*Ic value of polymer concrete (PC) materials. The research involved experimental investigations using five different testing techniques and specimen types, namely the single edge notched beam (SENB), short bend beam (SBB), semi-circular bend (SCB), edge notch disc bend (ENDB), and center cracked Brazilian disc (CCBD). A typical PC mixture made of mineral silicious aggregate, ML506 epoxy resin, chopped E-glass, and foundry sand filler. Despite the difference in the shape and loading type of the tested samples, the *K*Ic data obtained from all groups of specimens are in good agreement with together and with the SENB proposed by RILEM. Depending on the test type, the *K*Ic value varied from 1.43 to 1.74 MPa.m0.5 and the discrepancy between the data was mainly attributed to the type of loading (compression or bending) and the crack type (center crack or edge crack). The *T*-stress affects the fracture toughness for different testing samples and configurations. The lowest fracture toughness corresponds to the CCBD specimen (the center cracked disc loaded diametrically). The other test samples with edge cracks and loaded by a three-point bend setup showed *K*Ic = 1.7 - 1.74 MPa.m0.5. Moreover, the fracture toughness data for PC mixtures can be achieved by utilizing sub-sized samples like SBB (for smaller amounts of PC material) instead of larger beam samples (i.e., SENB). ## Keywords. results.title: Anisotropic fracture energy and toughness of single crystal gallium arsenide by microindentation - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Anisotropic fracture energy and toughness of single crystal gallium arsenide by microindentation. Although single crystal gallium arsenide (GaAs) is a technologically important semiconductor material, its mechanical behavior is poorly understood. In this study, the Vickers microindentation technique was leveraged with a quantitative fractographic approach to determine the fracture energy and toughness corresponding to various crystal planes. The literature is rich with linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) models that describe the fracture energy and toughness of linear, elastic, isotropic materials. Although some authors have employed indentation fracture mechanics to estimate the fracture toughness of select anisotropic materials, these estimates adapt LEFM approaches by homogenizing the material behavior, thereby glossing over the anisotropy. Unfortunately, these models cannot be readily applied to anisotropic materials, such as GaAs single crystals: no single accepted standard method currently exists to evaluate the directional fracture energy and toughness in anisotropic single crystals [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. Therefore the literature reports a wide range of fracture energy and toughness values for GaAs, with particular uncertainty in the cleavage plane and crack propagation directions. In the present study, we therefore combine mechanical indentation and fractography to quantify the crystalline anisotropy for single crystal GaAs. These experimental results are compared to the theoretical fracture energy calculated using a broken bonds model. For any crystallographic zone axis, the GaAs effective directional Young’s modulus (elastic stiffness) orthogonal to the crack propagation direction was calculated inside the crystallographic plane for the median crack system perpendicular to the indented (0 0 1) surface:where , and are the direction cosines of the angle between the crystallographic direction and the cubic crystal’s zone axis [27], [28]. Currently there is no consensus in the literature about how to determine the anisotropic fracture toughness and energy in single crystals using hardness indentation. There is also no consensus about which fracture criterion applies to crack initiation and propagation in single crystals: is the maximum tensile stress (MS-Criterion) or the maximum ERR (ME-Criterion) better suited to GaAs? ### Cohesive interface simulations of indentation cracking as a fracture toughness measurement method for brittle materials. ### Novel micro-scale specimens for mode-dependent fracture testing of brittle materials: A case study on GaAs single crystals.
